reason: Amber provides a working stateful manual watcher rather than a snapshot needing manual diff implementation. Its complete release set detects a new stable maintenance release below the greatest version, a counterexample the teal maximum-only implementation misses. These benefits were independently exercised with the actual answer code and no network or filesystem writes.

independently_checked_benefits.benefit: First-run baseline, unchanged repeat, local change detection and preservation of state on collection failure work in actual main() with an in-memory filesystem substitute.
independently_checked_benefits.verification: Extracted Python block, compiled/executed in memory. Injected deterministic collect() and FakePath/FakeOS. First two main() calls returned 0; baseline printed once and OK twice. Injected collection exception returned 1 and preserved byte-equivalent virtual state.

independently_checked_benefits.benefit: Detects an added stable lower-branch release that a latest-only snapshot misses.
independently_checked_benefits.verification: Mock PyPI files included 12.0.0 and 11.3.1 stable, a 13.0.0rc1 prerelease and yanked 10.0.0. Actual collect() retained exactly both eligible stable versions and an advisory across two pages. Adding 11.3.2 to the collected baseline printed REVIEW release:11.3.2. Actual teal stable() still returns 12.0.0. Synthetic failure-case check, not a claim of a currently missed real Pillow release.

limitations: Neither live end-to-end watcher was reproduced; terminal DNS unavailable.
Amber pilot covers upstream repository advisories, not package-wide OSV/global aggregation; this is explicitly disclosed.
Teal honestly labels baseline storage and deduplication as future work, but the requested watcher is less complete.
Both use a deliberately restricted numeric Pillow version convention.
Simulated tests establish defined failure cases and code behavior, not complete real-world service reliability.
